```text
Peak Poker Performance

What Does Your A Game Look Like?
It has been suspected as far back as in Socrates’ time that self-awareness
is a key aspect of high level performance. In the book entitled Emotional
Intelligence 2.0, Drs. Bradberry and Greaves wrote that 83% of top per-
formers but only 2% of bottom performers across a myriad of occupa-
tions were high in self-awareness. Self-awareness can be defined as “the
capacity to step outside your own skin and look at yourself with as close
to an objective eye as possible” (Rock, 2009). This ability can help you
overcome blind spots and improve more rapidly. In order to figure out
how to optimize your game, you have to learn how to assess what level
you are playing at.
    A performance continuum exists where you can play your A, B, C, D, or
F game, and each level is dynamic: your A game is going to change as you
get more experience in the game. The more technical expertise you gain,
the better decisions you’ll be capable of making. Being off your A game
occurs anytime you make a less than optimal decision than you are capa-
ble of in a given spot. Tony Schwartz, co-author of The Power of Full En-
gagement, considers that the A game is played when players are able to
show up with everything they have got.
    One experienced cash game player told me that he considers himself
on his A game when 90% or more of his decisions are the best decisions
that he can make in a given hand. He asks himself how confident he is
with the decision he made during each phase of every hand he chooses to
play. If, after taking into account hand ranges, table dynamics, and the
like, he is satisfied with his decision, then he has made an A level play.
Note that playing the A game is not about winning the hand. The result is
not the metric to determine this. Rather, you need to ask yourself if you
were 100% confident that your decisions were right given the informa-
tion you had to work with. If you feel unsure about whether or not a play
was correct, it is a sign that some technical homework is in order.
    If you are on your A game, you’ll notice you can process a great deal of
information quickly and easily. Your focus will be impeccable. You will be
able to put your opponents on accurate hand ranges, and you’ll under-
```

```text
                                              Deconstructing the A Game

stand their typical lines. Everything will flow, and you will make optimal

   Let’s consider the opposite end of the spectrum. You can consider your-
self on your F game whenever you find yourself missing important cues and
vital information. You’ll be prone to making mistakes when you are off your
game. When you are playing your F game you take shortcuts and don’t
think things through as thoroughly as you should. Even though you may
occasionally arrive at a correct decision, you are not playing well. How fully
you think through each situation is a strong indicator of the level of game
you are playing. If you are not able to think through a hand thoroughly to
determine the best decision, you are not anywhere near the A game.
   Each player has to figure out precisely what being off their A game
means to them. Most experienced players develop some sort of metric to
help them determine where they are on the grading scale and it is wise to
take time to develop your own rating system (Table 1). How do you think,
feel, and behave when you are playing your A game? How will you know if
you’ve slipped into your B game? How do your thoughts, emotions, and
behaviors change when you digress? How about the C level? Finally, what
do your D and F games look like?
```

```text
   The more time you spend noticing your thoughts, feelings, and behav-
iors, the more your self-awareness will increase. If you can get to the
point where you notice your experiences in real time, you’ll be more able
to make conscious choices about how you will respond, which will open
you up to achieving peak performance. If you are unaware, you’ll likely be
auto-piloting, which can lead to mistakes.

Flow as the Optimal Psychological State
I’ve had the opportunity to talk to a number of poker players about the A
game, and it’s usually described as having certain characteristics. When it
happens, you’ll find yourself fully engaged in an almost effortless per-
formance, making good decisions, and playing at your best. You know you
are in the zone when you:

   ♠ are fully immersed in the moment
   ♠ feel totally in control
   ♠ feel extremely self-confident
   ♠ are playing to the top of your capabilities.

    Robert Nideffer is a leading researcher on optimal performance states.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

there are several attributes that must be present if you want to increase
your likelihood of peak performance:

     ♠ You must be confident in your ability to be successful. Lack of
        confidence breeds self-doubt, which can lead to fear of failure.
        The best way to be confident is to be fully prepared and well
        trained for the games you are playing.
     ♠ You must be fully immersed in your present performance. You
        cannot be thinking about past hands you played or worrying about
        the future. You are seeking total “in the moment” concentration.
     ♠ You must only attend to those things which are directly related to
        playing poker.
     ♠ You must be able to ignore distractions, which capture your
        attention and disrupt automatic processing. If you do get
        distracted, get back on task as quickly as possible.


   Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (pronounced Me-high Cheek-sent-me-high),
the psychologist who calls this performance state flow, theorized about
what it takes to achieve peak performance in his book Flow (1990). He
said that if you want to get into flow, you must learn to focus your atten-
tion to such an extent that nothing else seems to matter. His studies indi-
cate that people who experience flow states are immersed in what
they’re doing so completely that they lose track of time. Furthermore,
they reported being totally at ease, extremely confident, and having total
and automatic concentration.
   We know that practice and preparation is important for peak physical
performance, but how does it relate to mental performance as in poker?
Steptoe (1998) found that mental skills can be enhanced by the prepara-
tion and practice of skills like automated problem solving, the flow of
ideas, and the identification of new ways to think about and do things.
Steptoe found that the development of a creative idea or a solution to a
problem doesn’t develop out of thin air. You have to have learned and be-
```

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/Peak%20Poker%20Performance.pdf#page=94)

```text
                                              Deconstructing the A Game

come comfortable with the individual ideas and pieces of information in
your domain in order to get into a flow state that allows you to manipu-
late your knowledge.
    Csikszentmihalyi also notes that flow can only happen when your skills
are matched to the opportunities for action. A mismatch between our
skills and our capabilities will render us bored or anxious. If you are at a
table stacked with opponents who outclass you, you will very likely feel
anxious. If you outclass your opponents, boredom will ensue. In either
case, it is not likely that you will be on your A game. Like Steptoe, Csik-
szentmihalyi believes that flow is the optimal state for performing. Flow
states happen when your skills are up to the challenge at hand. Further,
you should always put your attention on goals you can move towards. He
says that the most essential skill in life is to be able to “transform adver-
sity into an enjoyable challenge” (1990).
    Getting into a flow state requires that we learn to control our con-
sciousness. Research on flow is pretty clear about this one thing: we can
learn to manage whether or not we are in a flow state. As Csikszentmiha-
lyi (2008) describes it, “A person can make himself happy, or miserable,
regardless of what is actually happening on the outside, just by changing
the contents of consciousness.” If you can somehow manage to trans-
form situations that seem to be hopeless into challenges to overcome,
you’ll react more effectively.
    Think about yourself. When you are running bad, do you give up or do
you dig deep and try to figure out ways to overcome (or at least lessen)
your problems? If you have a tendency to think about overcoming obsta-
cles you are high in resilience. Our situations do not determine our state.
Csikszentmihalyi (2008) says it’s all about how we organize the contents
of our consciousness. He suggests that we organize the contents so that
we may often be in a state of flow. Learning to control your conscious-
ness is an inside job. It is not enough to know how to do it, one must do it!
    When you are on your A game, chances are you are in flow. If you are
not fully in a flow state you are at least experiencing elements of it. If you
are off your A game, by definition you cannot be in the zone.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

Pre-Game Considerations
There are several factors that contribute to performance that you should
consider before you start playing. Assessing these factors will help you
assess whether or not you are in a state where you are even capable of an
optimal performance:

     ♠ Is your mind in a clear state? Do you have things going on that
        could be distracting? Do you have other things that need your
        attention such as family obligations or even errands to run? Have
        you just had an argument with your significant other?
     ♠ Such things can keep you from focusing fully on poker. Before you
        start a session, make certain that you have time to play and have
        taken care of potential distractions.
     ♠ Are the games good for you? Is the table stacked with good
        regulars? If it is, assess your level of focus. If it is high and you are
        up for a challenge, consider sitting down. If not, perhaps look for a
        better game that is more compatible with where you are in your
        development and mindset.
     ♠ Are you motivated? This might sound silly, but are you truly
        motivated? Are you feeling good and ready to go?
     ♠ As there is no off season in poker, it is possible to overplay and
        become burned out and unmotivated. Don’t just go through the
        motions. A game performances are unlikely to occur during
        periods of de-motivation. Manage your energy wisely and choose
        times to play that coincide with your peak states.
     ♠ How is your self-knowledge? Do you know when you put in your
        best hours?
     ♠ Most people have certain times of the day or night when they are
        naturally at their peak. Track yours, and try to play when you are
        most likely to be fresh. If you track this long enough, you’ll see
        clear times of the day when you have the highest win rates.
```

```text
                                              Deconstructing the A Game

   ♠ Do you tend to play better at a certain casino? If you play online,
       what is the best set-up for you? Do you play best on a laptop,
       tablet, or desktop? Do you play best while seated or at a standing
       desk? Look at everything in order to determine which variables
       contribute to you playing your best.
   ♠ How does running especially good or bad affect your play?
   ♠ It’s hard not be too affected by winning or losing, so pay close
       attention to how these affect you. Be conscious of your states.
       Are you prone to chasing losses? How do you deal with losing, in
       general? If losing a couple of buy-ins makes you tilt, walk away;
       you are not on your A game. If you are winning, watch that you
       don’t play too loosely. Being up does not justify loose river calls,
       for example.


    As Csikszentmihalyi said, “It is not enough to know how to do it; one
must do it, consistently, in the same way as athletes or musicians must
keep practicing what they know in theory.” Only when you can do what
you know how to do, will you have the opportunity for peak performance.
    The bottom line is that you need to do everything in your power to put
yourself in situations where you can be fully present and fully focused on
playing your best. It is not easy to do, because we all have outside stress-
ors and distractions. Ruthlessly eliminate things that take you off course.
If that’s not possible, sitting out is often the best strategy. Otherwise, you
want to optimize your life and your game as much as possible, so that be-
ing focused and making good decisions is easier for you.
```
